title: Thanksgiving Dishes Seniors Can Bring to Family Dinner | GoGo Blog
summary: Eight Thanksgiving dishes seniors can bring to family dinner, each with a lighter swap, which ones travel well, and how to get the groceries delivered before the holiday.
body_markdown:
Someone always asks, "What can I bring?" If you're an older adult heading to a family dinner this year, the best Thanksgiving dishes to bring are the ones that travel well, don't need a last-minute oven, and taste like the holiday without the heavy salt, sugar, and butter that many doctors ask us to watch. Below are eight Thanksgiving meals for seniors that fit that bill, with a lighter twist on each, plus an easy way to get the ingredients to your kitchen when the stores are at their busiest.


If a grocery run before the holiday is the hard part, GoGo Grocery can help get the ingredients on your list delivered to your door. Call 1 (855) 464-6872 and press 7 for delivery, and a personal shopper places the grocery delivery order for you. More on that at the end.


## **What makes a Thanksgiving dish healthier for seniors?**


You don't need special recipes. A few swaps in the dishes you already love go a long way when you're cooking holiday recipes for seniors:


**Salt.** The[CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/salt/about/index.html) says eating too much sodium can raise blood pressure. Season with garlic, black pepper, fresh herbs, lemon, or a little ginger instead of reaching for the salt shaker a second time.


**Sugar.** If you or a guest manages diabetes, less added sugar matters. If you'd like to use less, choose a recipe written that way. In sides like mashed sweet potatoes, taste before adding any sweetener. You may find they're sweet enough on their own.


**Butter.** If your doctor has asked you to watch saturated fat, olive oil in place of some of the butter is an easy swap in mashed potatoes, roasted vegetables, and gravy.


One note before you change anything: health needs differ. Some people are told to eat more salt, not less, and some eating plans are built around butter. When in doubt, ask your doctor which swaps make sense for you.


## **What should you ask the host before you choose a dish?**


A two-minute phone call to whoever is hosting saves a lot of guesswork, and it usually settles which of the Thanksgiving dishes to bring is the right one for you. Ask how many people are coming, whether anyone at the table has an allergy or a diet to work around, and whether there will be oven or stovetop space when you arrive, because a crowded kitchen on Thanksgiving afternoon is the normal state of things. If the answer is no, choose something that reheats in a microwave or is eaten as it is, like rolls or cranberry sauce. It's also worth asking what's already covered, since three bowls of mashed sweet potatoes is a real risk in a big family. Once you know the gaps, pick from the list below.


## **What are the best Thanksgiving dishes to bring?**


### **1. Herb-roasted turkey breast**


If you've been asked to bring the main event, turkey breast is the easiest cut to handle: it's lean protein, it roasts in a single pan, and it slices neatly at the table without the carving performance a whole bird demands. Rub it with rosemary, sage, lemon zest, and olive oil, and you get plenty of flavor without extra salt. Cook it to 165°F. If dinner is a short drive away, carry it in a covered dish and bring it over close to mealtime. If dinner is still a while off, ask the host to make room in the fridge when you arrive. And if carrying a turkey sounds like more work than you want, a bag of bakery rolls is an easy thing to bring.


### **2. Roasted vegetables**


Roasted vegetables are among the simplest healthy meals for seniors to make for a crowd. Brussels sprouts, carrots, beets, and winter squash all bring fiber and vitamins, and they crisp up beautifully in the oven. Chop (or buy them pre-cut), toss with olive oil and pepper, and roast. They're just as good at room temperature, which makes them a good dish to carry across town.


Try[this roasted vegetable recipe](https://itdoesnttastelikechicken.com/the-best-roasted-vegetables-for-thanksgiving/) with crunchy nuts for a Thanksgiving-worthy side.


### **3. Mashed sweet potatoes**


Sweet potatoes bring beta-carotene, which your body turns into vitamin A, along with fiber. Mash them with olive oil or a small amount of butter, fresh rosemary, and black pepper. Taste before adding any sweetener; they're often sweet enough on their own. They reheat well, so they can be made the day before.


For a step-by-step version, see this[mashed sweet potatoes recipe from Love and Lemons](https://www.loveandlemons.com/mashed-sweet-potatoes/) .


### **4. Green bean casserole**


Green bean casserole is a favorite, and the usual version leans on canned soup and a lot of sodium. Green beans themselves bring fiber and vitamins, so the fix is the sauce. Make a lighter one with sautéed mushrooms and onions, a little flour, and low-fat or non-dairy milk, then top with whole-wheat panko instead of fried onions.


This[recipe from Well Plated](https://www.wellplated.com/healthy-green-bean-casserole/) keeps the classic taste without the canned soup.


### **5. Whole wheat rolls**


Rolls are the dish nobody minds you bringing. Switching from white to whole wheat is one of the easiest swaps in holiday recipes for seniors: the whole grain keeps its bran and germ, which is where the[B vitamins and vitamin E](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/what-should-you-eat/whole-grains/) live. A bakery bag of whole wheat rolls counts. So does a bread machine loaf.


### **6. Lighter gravy**


Gravy is a Thanksgiving staple and a hidden source of fat and salt. For a lighter version, use low-sodium chicken broth and thicken it with arrowroot or tapioca starch instead of a butter-and-flour roux. Carry it in a jar and warm it on the stove when you arrive.


This[starch-thickened gravy recipe from 40 Aprons](https://40aprons.com/paleo-gravy-easy-whole30/) is a good starting point. It still uses some fat, so follow your own doctor's advice on how much.


### **7. Real cranberry sauce**


Canned cranberry sauce is mostly sugar. Homemade is not hard: fresh cranberries, a splash of orange juice, and a small amount of sweetener, far less than the canned kind uses, simmered until they pop. It keeps in the fridge for days and travels in any container with a lid.


Try this[cranberry sauce from Cookie and Kate](https://cookieandkate.com/naturally-sweetened-cranberry-sauce-recipe/) , which skips refined sugar.


### **8. Pumpkin pie**


No Thanksgiving is complete without pie. Pumpkin is a good choice among the desserts because the filling brings vitamin A and fiber, and a lighter version uses less sugar and evaporated or non-dairy milk instead of heavy cream. If baking has gotten tiring, a store-bought pie with a fresh fruit bowl beside it is a fine contribution too. More ideas in our guide to the[healthiest fruits for seniors](https://www.gogograndparent.com/blog/8-healthiest-fruits-for-seniors-to-upgrade-your-wellness) .

If you no longer drive, a dish that travels well still needs a ride. GoGo can arrange one. ## **Healthy Thanksgiving meals for seniors are easier than they sound**


A few swaps and a little planning are all it takes. Pick one or two dishes from this list, order the ingredients early, and let the delivery and the ride be someone else's job this year. That leaves more of the day for the people at the table.

## **FAQ**


### **What Thanksgiving dishes travel well?**


Rolls, cranberry sauce, and pie travel in any container with a lid. Roasted vegetables, mashed sweet potatoes, gravy, and casseroles travel well in a covered dish for a short drive and can be warmed up when you arrive; if dinner is still a while off, ask the host for fridge space. Avoid dishes that need to be served the moment they come out of the oven.


### **What can a senior bring to Thanksgiving if they don't cook much?**


A bakery bag of whole wheat rolls, a store-bought pumpkin pie with a bowl of fresh fruit, or homemade cranberry sauce, which takes about fifteen minutes on the stove. Showing up with something is what matters, and nobody has ever turned away rolls.
